nb_glen_falls.blurb: A small bolted crag in the east end of Saint John, close enough to town for a quick evening session. Its thirteen sport lines run from an easy slab up through the middle grades, with most falling between roughly 5.6 and 5.10 and a single 5.11 for the strong. The wall faces south, so it picks up plenty of sun and dries fast after rain, and the stone is well featured with decent friction. Expect everything from low-angle slabs to steeper overhanging sections. Draws are all you need, though a couple of longer ones help on the lines that run out. A short walk gets you to the base.

nb_main_face.blurb: The Main Face is the first cliff you meet on the hike up Mount Douglas, near Welsford, and it sits in front of the town's golf course. It holds a dozen routes, mostly trad with a couple of bolted lines, and the grades start around 5.8 with the bulk in the 5.8 to 5.12 range. The rock is granite, and the face is known for a good hand crack alongside steeper, more demanding lines. The walk in from the car is a modest uphill trail, and the face tends to be quiet, making it a reasonable stop for a trad climber comfortable with mid to hard grades.

nb_the_great_roof_area.blurb: One of four sections of Eagle Rock, an early-developed trad cliff near Welsford beside Highway 7. This section has twelve routes, nearly all trad plus a single aid line, and the grades spread widely: a few easy lines, a handful around 5.7 and 5.8, then a hard cluster of 5.10 and 5.11 climbs, including a roof finger crack. Gear skills matter more than clipping stamina here. Reaching the wall means a short walk along the road from the picnic area to a flagged trail that climbs gently through woods. Good for a climber wanting a mix of moderate trad and a couple of serious testpieces.

nb_utopia_wall.blurb: The main overhanging wall at Utopia, a steep sport crag about an hour and a half from Fredericton. Twelve bolted routes tackle a big overhang split by flaring grooves that call for inventive sequences, with an easy slab at one end and a few moderate lines nearby. Most of the difficulty sits in the 5.12 and 5.13 range, so this is mainly a destination for strong climbers, with only a few lines below 5.11. The wall gets sun in the morning and shade later in the day. Some rock to the right is crumbly, so a helmet is wise, and some lines seep in wet weather. The approach is only a few minutes on a flagged trail.

nb_sea_monster_area.blurb: An ice and mixed cliff in Walton Glen canyon, on the Fundy coast side of the Little Salmon River country. Eleven lines, mostly steep water ice, with a few traditional mixed routes mixed in. Grades run from WI3 into WI5, with the majority around WI4 and a single harder WI5 line. The walls face northeast and see very little sun, which keeps the ice in condition through the winter. Descent is by rappel from trees near the stream, and a 70 m rope can nearly reach the ground in one go, though two shorter rappels are recommended. This is a committing winter outing in a remote setting.

nb_x_wall.blurb: A trad wall on McQuirks Mountain, a forested hillside near Fredericton just up the road from Utopia. The dozen routes here are all gear-protected and mostly one or two pitches, with a good spread of difficulty: a few climbs around 5.7 and 5.8, a solid group of 5.10s, and one hard 5.12 line at the top end. Lines head straight up the face, with some slabby sections where careful footwork pays off. The walk in is a mixed-forest trail of around half an hour, following an established path. It is a quiet spot that suits parties wanting moderate to mid-grade trad.
